title: Make with AI on My Cuff or Bag
sentence: Choose a source detail, arrange materials, compare prepared AI effects on a cuff or bag picture, then select a postcard.
rq: During material arrangement and AI cuff/bag previews, how do participants maintain or revise their sense of authenticity?
purpose: A connects three things: a detail from a named heritage object, a material arrangement, and an AI adaptation shown on an everyday-item picture. The questionnaire asks what kept or changed what felt authentic, and why.
steps: Choose a source detail
Look at the object image and checked information. Choose a line, shape or other detail to explore.
Arrange materials
Use paper, shapes, fabric or simple objects to interpret the detail. Help is available.
View a prepared example
The researcher shows the closest prepared example linking a sample layout and source detail to an AI effect on a cuff or bag picture.
Adjust and compare
Change the arrangement and compare another prepared example. These images illustrate sample layouts.
Choose your postcard
Select a card showing the source and preferred effect. The anonymous card joins the shared local wall after submission.
Reflect and keep a copy
Answer the optional authenticity question. You may take a printed copy of your own postcard.
ai: AI creates the example adaptations before the session. The researcher checks them, then manually switches between prepared examples during the activity. Participants are told how the simulation works. The example is matched to a sample layout and source detail.
noai: Participants can skip an activity or question, stop, or discard drafts before submission. A separate non-AI comparison condition is a possible future study design.
theory: Relational authenticity draws attention to connections among people, objects, making and history. In this test, the participant’s written reflection explains which connection mattered.
Looking alike and having a real link
A similar shape and knowledge of a maker or history offer different grounds for authenticity. The questionnaire invites participants to describe the grounds they use.
Embodied-generation precedents motivate the material activity. Prepared examples let this first-stage study explore how people understand the idea and what they want to change.
future: Design possibility for later development: a museum shares changing textile patterns for everyday cuffs and bags. What connections to the source would people want to keep visible?
speculation: The book cases help us imagine this arrangement and decide what the examples should communicate. The submitted first-stage protocol uses material exploration, postcard selection and the questionnaire. A separate future-label discussion would belong to a later plan.
record: Keep the selected source-detail and prepared-image references for the submitted A card. The written evidence comes from the anonymous questionnaire. Physical arrangements, photographs, observation notes and interaction logs are outside this first-stage data collection.
analysis: Read the authenticity reflections alongside the selected source and example references. Summarise reasons about resemblance, source context, material exploration and personal connection. Compare development preferences and suggestions across the two activities.
value: This development study helps choose which direction to refine. A later study could examine how source-related judgments develop during a working AI interaction. The current written reflections help identify useful questions and design choices.
setup: Source images and information for the agreed objects, simple arranging materials, checked prepared AI examples, a screen, a local postcard wall and optional printing.
broad: No museum or AI expertise is required. Simple materials and researcher help support participation. First-stage recruitment is restricted to adult ECS staff and students who can understand the study information and give consent.
checkpoint: Use questionnaire reasons and selected-example references to identify unclear steps, meaningful source connections and useful improvements. Record suggestions through the questionnaire.

title: One Object, Two Interpretations
sentence: Write your interpretation, choose a prepared AI image, and place both on one postcard. Read earlier cards and add a reply or clarification.
rq: During AI-mediated cross-cultural exchange, how do participants maintain, question or clarify their meaning through others' responses?
purpose: B brings the source, a person’s exact words and an AI image into one shared postcard. Earlier participants’ cards give later participants something specific to respond to. Anonymous cards and replies accumulate on the same local wall used by A.
steps: Read the source and earlier cards
Look at the object information and submitted postcards already on the local wall. Prepared starter notes are clearly labelled.
Write in your own words
Express an interpretation in any language and choose a prepared AI image. Typing help is available.
Make one postcard
The researcher manually places your exact words, source reference and chosen image together in one whiteboard postcard.
Reply or clarify
Read another card and add a reply, or clarify a meaning. People can keep different interpretations.
Check and submit
Check drafts with the researcher for identifying details. Submitted anonymous cards remain for later participants to read.
Reflect and keep your card
Answer the optional cross-cultural question. You may take a printed copy of your own card without other people’s replies.
ai: AI images and labelled multilingual starter notes and example translations are prepared before sessions. The researcher assembles the cards manually. Participants’ original words are kept as written and are not sent to AI services.
noai: Participants may skip the activity, a reply or a questionnaire question, and discard drafts before submission. The current study uses prepared AI content to explore the concept.
theory: Relational authenticity helps us consider how an object connects people and experiences. B’s submitted text and replies give a first account of these connections.
Personal voice and recognition help us distinguish what someone wanted to express from how another person responded. Their original words stay visible on the postcard.

Research on language agency and cultural detail motivates keeping original words and allowing clarification. Prepared multilingual examples introduce the wider design idea. Participants’ live text remains unchanged by AI.
future: Design possibility for later development: a museum displays visitor interpretations together with the replies that helped shape them. Whose words should appear, and what should a later visitor see?
speculation: The shared postcard offers a concrete object for imagining how visitor interpretations might be displayed in a museum. The first-stage protocol collects submitted cards and questionnaire responses. Further speculative discussions would need their own planned questions.
record: Keep submitted original postcard text, replies and clarifications with source-detail, prepared-image and reply references. Keep questionnaire answers separately from the wall. Prepared AI starter notes are labelled and excluded from participant data.
analysis: Summarise themes in the questionnaire and submitted card text about expression, understanding, clarification, AI images and the shared wall. Use the reply relationships to read exchanges in context. Participants’ language choices provide context without assigning national identities.
value: The study helps refine a postcard activity for cultural expression and exchange. Original text and replies show what people chose to say in this setting. A later working system could examine live translation and generation with a separately specified procedure.
setup: One local digital postcard wall on study equipment, source images and information, prepared AI images, labelled starter notes, manual card assembly and optional printing.
broad: Use any language for postcard text. Researcher help is available for entering exact words. Adult ECS staff or students can join individually and respond to an earlier submitted card. The first-stage study requires no account or personal device.
checkpoint: Use the card text, replies and questionnaire to identify where the image supports expression, where an interpretation invites clarification, and how to improve the activity and shared wall.
